analysis.one_liner: Blocks state and local restrictions on FDA-approved reproductive health products, like abortion pills and contraception.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate on August 2, 2022, two months after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, the bill was sent to the Judiciary Committee the same day and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop any state or local government from enforcing a restriction on the use or purchase of reproductive health products approved or authorized by the FDA — including abortion pills, contraception, and other pregnancy-related drugs and devices. Patients and health care providers could sue to stop such restrictions, and the Justice Department could sue states as well. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who need FDA-approved reproductive health products — particularly people in states that have moved to ban or restrict medication abortion, contraception, or related drugs since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade — and the health care providers who serve them. The bill gives both a federal court path to strike down state restrictions, with the winning side's attorney's fees paid.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients in states restricting reproductive care

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits any state, local government, or official acting under color of law from enforcing a law that restricts use of or access to any FDA-approved drug or device used to diagnose, prevent, manage, treat, or terminate a pregnancy, or to manage conditions of the reproductive system.

Patients and health care providers adversely affected by a state restriction can file suit in federal court for injunctive relief, and prevailing plaintiffs receive their costs and attorney's fees; the Justice Department can also sue states on the country's behalf.
The bill authorizes $20 million to the Attorney General to enforce the ban on state restrictions.

analysis.who_pays: State governments would lose the power to restrict or regulate these products, and federal taxpayers would fund Justice Department enforcement, authorized at $20 million.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state law across a broad area of health regulation long governed by states, which raises federalism objections that courts would likely have to resolve; opponents would argue Congress lacks authority to override state health and criminal law this way.

The bill only covers drugs and devices approved or cleared by the FDA. It does not protect access to surgical abortion procedures or other non-drug care, so its real-world coverage is narrower than its name suggests.
Enforcement would require ongoing federal litigation in many states, funded by a $20 million authorization that Congress would have to appropriate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients in restrictive states, the bill would have created a powerful legal tool to keep FDA-approved abortion pills and contraception available, with fees shifting to make suits affordable for providers and patients. The main objections are constitutional (broad federal preemption of state health law) and practical (it would not cover surgical abortion, and it would draw years of court fights). The bill never advanced far enough for those questions to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill on August 2, 2022, with Senator Tina Smith, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action appears in the bill's history — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill had five cosponsors: four Senate Democrats and one Senate Independent, in a Senate with 48 Democrats, 2 Independents, and 50 Republicans.

The bill was introduced two months after the Supreme Court's Dobbs decision overturned Roe v. Wade, when several states began restricting or banning medication abortion — a use the bill's preemption language would have blocked.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State officials who restrict or ban abortion pills and contraception keep that power, because no federal preemption exists. People in restrictive states gained no guaranteed federal protection for access to these products.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State officials with abortion and contraception restrictions

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on August 2, 2022.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee where the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on August 2, 2022 and took no recorded action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no roll-call split exists; every recorded supporter was a Democrat or the Independent sponsor of the pair, with no Republican cosponsors.

industries.industry: Pharmaceutical makers of reproductive health drugs (contraception, medication abortion)
industries.note: The bill would have guaranteed a national market for FDA-approved reproductive health drugs by blocking state restrictions, and patients would have gained the same guaranteed access. Its failure leaves state-by-state limits in place for both the industry and patients.

industries.industry: Health care providers, including clinics prescribing medication abortion
industries.note: Providers would have gained a federal court action, with attorney's fees, to strike down state restrictions affecting their staff and patients.
Pharmacies dispensing FDA-approved reproductive health drugs would have operated free of state-level bans or penalties, alongside the patients they serve.
